title: What Is Amazon Web Services?
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of what is amazon web services? and its relationship to Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to what is amazon web services?.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn what is amazon web services? in the context of Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: What Is Amazon Web Services? matters because it is one part of cloud concepts and service selection. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** What Is Amazon Web Services? belongs to Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing. Start from the cloud model, then learn how to describe a workload and map its needs to AWS service categories.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Definition of AWS; AWS services and infrastructure; AWS customers and use cases. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For what is amazon web services?, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Definition of AWS
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: AWS services and infrastructure
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: AWS customers and use cases
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “What Is Amazon Web Services?”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for What Is Amazon Web Services? with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: What Is Amazon Web Services? is taught as part of Introduction to AWS and Cloud Computing.
Start from the cloud model, then learn how to describe a workload and map its needs to AWS service categories.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
